title: Cauchy–Green boundary formula on an annulus
statement: Use $\mathbf R,\mathbf C$ [def-weil-field] with planar Lebesgue measure $dA$. Let $c\in\mathbf C$, let $0<r<R$, let $V\subset\mathbf C$ be open and contain $A=\{\zeta:r\leq|\zeta-c|\leq R\}$, and let $v:V\to\mathbf C$ have continuous first partial derivatives in real coordinates. Define $\partial_{\bar\zeta}v=\tfrac12(\partial_xv+i\partial_yv)$. Then $$\int_A\partial_{\bar\zeta}v\,dA=\frac1{2i}\left(\oint_{|\zeta-c|=R}v(\zeta)\,d\zeta-\oint_{|\zeta-c|=r}v(\zeta)\,d\zeta\right).$$ The area and line integrals are absolutely convergent. Both circles in this formula are counterclockwise, with $\zeta=c+se^{it}$, $0\leq t\leq2\pi$, for $s=R,r$.

proof.text: Identify $\mathbf C$ with $\mathbf R^2$ by $z=x+iy$. The continuous-partials criterion gives continuity of $v$ and the real differential $Dv(z)[h]=v_x(z)\operatorname{Re}h+v_y(z)\operatorname{Im}h$ on the open set $V$, with continuous coefficient functions. In particular $\partial_{\bar z}v=(v_x+iv_y)/2$ is continuous. This uses exactly the stated continuous coordinate partials, and does not assume that $v$ is holomorphic or infinitely differentiable.

proof.text: The annulus $A$ is a closed bounded subset of $\mathbf R^2$, hence compact. The compact-integrability lemma applied to $\partial_{\bar z}v|_A$ proves absolute convergence of the area integral. For $s=r,R$, the function $t\mapsto is e^{it}v(c+se^{it})$ is continuous on each of the compact intervals $[-\pi,\pi]$ and $[0,2\pi]$; the same lemma in dimension one proves absolute convergence of the parametrized line integrals. The norm of its factor $is e^{it}$ is $s$, so this is absolute convergence with respect to arc length as well.

proof.text: Put $Q=[r,R]\times[-\pi,\pi]$, $\Phi(\rho,t)=c+\rho e^{it}$, $w=v\circ\Phi$, $B=i\rho e^{it}w$ and $P=e^{it}w$. These functions are defined on the open set $\Phi^{-1}(V)$ containing $Q$. With $e^{it}=\cos t+i\sin t$, differentiating the coordinate functions gives $\Phi_\rho=e^{it}$ and $\Phi_t=i\rho e^{it}$. The pointwise real chain and product rules therefore give $w_\rho=(v_x\circ\Phi)\cos t+(v_y\circ\Phi)\sin t$ and $w_t=\rho(-(v_x\circ\Phi)\sin t+(v_y\circ\Phi)\cos t)$. Subtracting the product-rule formulas yields $$B_\rho-P_t=i\rho e^{it}w_\rho-e^{it}w_t=\rho\bigl(i(v_x\circ\Phi)-(v_y\circ\Phi)\bigr)=2i\rho(\partial_{\bar z}v)\circ\Phi.$$ The cancellation uses $e^{it}(i\cos t+\sin t)=i$ and $e^{it}(i\sin t-\cos t)=-1$. The only rules taken from the cited calculus node are its pointwise derivative rules, which apply to existing derivatives; its smoothness assertions are not applied to the merely $C^1$ function $v$.

proof.text: Apply the rectangle divergence formula with $F=B$, $G=-P$, $a=(r,-\pi)$ and $b=(R,\pi)$. The real differentials computed in the previous step give $L=DB$ and $M=-DP$ on $Q$. They may be extended arbitrarily outside their open domain since the rectangle formula uses only values on $Q$. Continuity of $v,v_x,v_y$ makes $F,G$ continuous on $Q$ and $H=B_\rho-P_t$ continuous there; the compact-integrability lemma supplies its required integrability. Since $e^{i\pi}=e^{-i\pi}=-1$, we have $P(\rho,\pi)=P(\rho,-\pi)$ pointwise, so the two radial-edge integrals cancel. The formula becomes $$\int_Q2i\rho(\partial_{\bar z}v)(\Phi(\rho,t))\,d\rho\,dt=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}B(R,t)\,dt-\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}B(r,t)\,dt.$$ The hypotheses $r<R$ and $-\pi<\pi$ give the required ordering of endpoints.

proof.text: Extend $h=1_A\partial_{\bar z}v$ by zero to $\mathbf C$. It is integrable by step 2. Apply the centered polar integration identity to $h$. On its target $T=(0,\infty)\times(-\pi,\pi)$, the condition $\Phi(\rho,t)\in A$ is exactly $r\leq\rho\leq R$, since $|\rho e^{it}|=\rho$. Hence $$\int_A\partial_{\bar z}v\,dA=\int_{[r,R]\times(-\pi,\pi)}\rho(\partial_{\bar z}v)(\Phi(\rho,t))\,d\rho\,dt=\int_Q\rho(\partial_{\bar z}v)(\Phi(\rho,t))\,d\rho\,dt.$$ The last change adds only the two angle edges, which have product Lebesgue measure zero (a finite interval times a singleton). The integrand is continuous and bounded on $Q$, so its integral over those edges is zero. Taking the constant $2i$ outside this integral identifies the left side of step 4 with $2i\int_A\partial_{\bar z}v\,dA$. No holomorphic annulus theorem is being used.

source.place: Agent polar-coordinate reduction to integral_divergence_prod_Icc_of_hasFDerivAt_of_le, lines 482–494; the annulus argument is supplied here, not stated by that theorem.

proof.text: For $s=r,R$ the function $B(s,t)=is e^{it}v(c+se^{it})$ is $2\pi$-periodic. Split its integral over $[-\pi,\pi]$ at zero, and in the part over $[-\pi,0]$ substitute $u=t+2\pi$. Periodicity changes that part into the integral over $[\pi,2\pi]$; adding the part over $[0,\pi]$ gives the integral over $[0,2\pi]$. By the parametrization in the statement this is precisely the counterclockwise integral $\oint_{|z-c|=s}v(z)\,dz$, because $\frac{d}{dt}(c+se^{it})=is e^{it}$. Step 4 and step 5 thus give $2i\int_A\partial_{\bar z}v\,dA=\oint_{|z-c|=R}v\,dz-\oint_{|z-c|=r}v\,dz$. Divide by $2i\ne0$. The inner integral has a minus sign while both parametrizations run counterclockwise, as required.
